exit_trigger: Evidence of brand pricing power eroding (volume losses after price increases, private label taking durable share); Management destroying value through poor acquisitions or buybacks at inflated prices; Discovery that debt or other obligations are materially larger than the reported debt-to-equity implies; Price exceeding 1.5× a re-verified intrinsic value for a persistent period
rationale: A packaged-food company is a business I can explain in two paragraphs, and the numbers in front of me look attractive: a 5-year average ROE of 25.3%, a debt-to-equity of 0.07, and a price of $34.29 against a model intrinsic value of $72.42. But a 52.6% discount on a brand I'd call a good, not great, franchise makes me ask what the market sees that I don't. I can't verify ten years of earnings, management tenure, or the debt picture from this snapshot, and a debt-to-equity that low looks odd to me for a food company, so I won't treat it as established. Until I've checked those, I'll keep my hands in my pockets and put this on the watch list rather than buy on the fields that happen to be present.

exit_trigger: Evidence that AI-driven automation is compressing pricing or utilization in core services; Loss of pricing power or falling client retention; Management destroying value through large acquisitions at poor prices; Price above 1.5x a conservatively re-estimated intrinsic value
rationale: Accenture screens well on the numbers I was given: a five-year average ROE of 27.7%, debt-to-equity of 0.003, and a computed margin of safety of 32.6% against an intrinsic value of $382.89 per share. But the snapshot gives me nothing about the business itself, so I cannot verify that the moat is durable. The question I keep asking is whether AI and automation will make this kind of consulting and outsourcing work cheaper to deliver and harder to charge for. A 5% discount rate and 8% growth rate also do much of the work in that valuation, and I would want to test it more conservatively. I will not write a check on a good-looking spreadsheet alone, so I watch and wait until I can check the earnings history, the moat evidence and management.

exit_trigger: Evidence that returns on equity are regressing toward market averages, indicating moat erosion; Debt-to-equity rising above 0.5 through debt-funded buybacks or acquisitions; Management capital allocation failures or evidence of dishonest reporting; Price exceeding 1.5x a conservatively re-estimated intrinsic value on a persistent basis
rationale: The numbers in front of me look attractive: a 5-year average ROE of about 30.6%, debt-to-equity of 0.497, and a computed margin of safety of roughly 38% against an intrinsic value of $1,271.73 per share. But a price is only half of what I need, and the snapshot gives me no business description, no earnings history, no management record and no evidence on the moat. I will not buy what I cannot explain in two paragraphs from the facts in hand, and I will not lean on a name or my memory to fill the gap. The debt-to-equity ratio sits right at my 0.5 ceiling with almost no room to spare, and the valuation rests on an 8% growth rate and a 5% discount rate that I would want to stress. I'll keep this on the watch list and wait until the missing evidence is in hand. No pitch is forced on me.

exit_trigger: Not applicable. No position taken.; Would revisit only if evidence emerges of durable pricing power or a structural cost advantage that persists across a full product cycle
rationale: I understand the business: Best Buy sells other people's electronics to consumers. That is where my trouble starts. I can't point to a moat here. It resells products it doesn't make, in a category where customers can compare prices in seconds, and the products themselves change fast. The numbers in front of me look respectable: a 48.4% five-year average ROE, a debt-to-equity of 0.39, and an 18.9% discount to a zero-growth owner-earnings value. But a cheap price on a business without a durable franchise is the cigar-butt mistake I made with Berkshire's textile mill. I'll pass and wait for a better pitch.

exit_trigger: Evidence of brand pricing power eroding, such as sustained discounting; Management capital allocation failures or evidence of dishonesty; Earnings history showing declines that contradict the quality thesis
rationale: Lululemon sells premium athletic apparel, and I can describe that in two paragraphs, so it sits inside my circle. The snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of 34.6%, debt-to-equity of 0.0, and a market cap of about $11.8 billion. The model's $347 per share intrinsic value against a $107 price looks too good, and I distrust a number that generous. It rests on 8% growth at a 5% discount rate, and it is built from owner earnings that I cannot verify here. What I cannot check is whether the brand is fashion-driven and must be rebuilt every season. Nothing here shows 10 years of positive earnings, pricing power, retention, or management quality. So I am not buying yet. I will wait until I can answer those questions, because a wide margin of safety on an unchecked moat is not a margin of safety at all.

exit_trigger: Not applicable - no position. I would revisit if evidence of a durable moat, a 10-year record of positive earnings and a capable management team emerged, together with at least a 15% margin of safety on a conservative growth assumption.
rationale: The numbers in front of me are respectable: a 5-year average ROE of 23.8%, debt-to-equity of 0.39, and a price about 18% below the model's intrinsic value. But I never buy a number, I buy a moat, and nothing in this snapshot shows me one. Retailing cars is a business where the customer can shop the next dealer down the road, and I have no evidence of pricing power or a cost advantage here. The snapshot also gives me no 10-year earnings record, no management data and no moat metrics, and the valuation assumes 0% growth with a 5% discount rate, so I won't call it a bargain. I'll keep this on the watch list and sit on my hands until I can show a durable competitive edge, and I'm not paying for a statistical discount alone.

exit_trigger: Evidence of brand erosion: sustained volume declines or loss of pricing power to private label; Deteriorating returns on capital or margins that signal the moat is being rebuilt rather than defended; Management destroys value through poor acquisitions or buybacks at inflated prices; Leverage rises materially above the 0.5 debt-to-equity threshold; Price exceeds 1.5x intrinsic value with the gap persisting
rationale: I understand a packaged-food company: it makes shelf-stable brands, sells them through grocers, and lives or dies on pricing power and shelf space. On the numbers in front of me the price looks cheap. The snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of 21.7%, a reported debt-to-equity of 0.19, and a 51% margin of safety against a zero-growth owner-earnings valuation. But a cheap price is not enough. The snapshot gives me no 10-year earnings record, no management or tenure data, and no evidence that the brand moat is holding against private label and changing eating habits. A low price on a business whose moat I cannot verify is how I ended up owning Berkshire's textile mill. I won't buy on the fields that happen to look good; I'll put it on the watch list until the gaps are filled.

exit_trigger: Evidence of eroding pricing power or gross margins versus competitors; Loss of customers or market share to online or larger-scale distributors; Debt-to-equity rising materially above 0.5; Management destroying value through poor acquisitions or buybacks at peak prices; Price exceeding 1.5x intrinsic value with a persistent gap
rationale: MSM is a distributor of industrial supplies, and I can explain that in two paragraphs, so I'll put it inside my circle. The numbers in front of me look good: a 5-year average ROE of 20.0%, debt-to-equity of 0.35, and a price of $121.02 against my $157.18 estimate, a 23% margin of safety. But the snapshot does not give me the evidence I need on the moat, on ten years of earnings history, or on management, and I won't buy on the fields that happen to be present. The low-cost, scale-and-service moat is a judgment I can't verify from this data, since gross margins and share trends aren't reported. The valuation also rests on 8% growth and a 5% discount rate, which are generous assumptions. I'd rather watch this pitch go by and wait until I can confirm the franchise.
